title: OT/ICS Security: the Purdue Model and Segmentation
oneLiner: Why plant networks need a different security approach: the Purdue model's levels, the industrial DMZ between office and plant, zones and conduits, and which traffic should never be allowed.
keyTakeaway: Industrial control systems put safety and availability first, run for decades, and often speak protocols with no authentication, so the network has to protect them. Split the plant into zones by function (the Purdue levels), put an industrial DMZ between IT and OT so nothing crosses directly, allow only the specific flows that are needed, and broker all remote access.
explanation:
OT (operational technology) is the hardware and software that monitors and controls physical processes: PLCs, HMIs, SCADA systems, drives and safety systems. An ICS (industrial control system) is the whole arrangement. OT security differs from office IT security in its priorities: a stopped line or an unsafe machine is worse than a leaked file, so safety and availability come first. Equipment runs for 15 to 25 years, patches wait for planned shutdowns and vendor approval, and many industrial protocols, Modbus among them, accept commands from anyone who can reach the device. Attacks such as Stuxnet (2010), the Ukrainian power grid attacks (2015 and 2016) and Triton (2017, aimed at safety controllers) showed what's at stake.

The Purdue model (from the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture) is the standard way to describe a plant network in levels. Level 0 is the physical process (sensors, valves, motors), Level 1 the controllers, Level 2 supervisory systems such as HMIs and engineering workstations, Level 3 site-wide operations such as the historian and MES (manufacturing execution system). Levels 4 and 5 are the business network and the outside world. Between Levels 3 and 4 sits Level 3.5, the industrial DMZ (demilitarized zone): a buffer where IT and OT systems meet without either connecting directly to the other. Office users read a historian mirror in the DMZ; vendors land on a jump host there.

IEC 62443, the main international standard family for industrial cybersecurity, turns this into zones (groups of assets with the same security needs) and conduits (the controlled paths between zones). In practice that means VLANs and firewalls between zones, allowlisted flows only, no traffic skipping levels, no internet access from control networks, controlled removable media, monitoring for unusual industrial traffic, and remote access brokered through the DMZ with MFA, approval and session recording. Place the systems below on their levels, then decide which flows the firewalls should allow.
